strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: fully quantized 4-bit training for LLMs, which is critical for reducing the enormous cost of pretraining.

It proposes a coherent set of techniques—unbiased double-block NVFP4 linear layers, OsciReset for weight oscillation suppression, and OutControl for outlier retention—with clear algorithmic descriptions and ablation studies.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: three model sizes (70M, 150M, 370M) and three data scales (50B, 100B, 200B tokens), with both perplexity and downstream task metrics. TetraJet-v2 consistently outperforms prior FP4 methods (Quartet and NVIDIA's recipe) across these settings.

The analysis of weight oscillation in LLM pretraining is novel and insightful. The paper introduces a clear metric (OsciRisk) and demonstrates the phenomenon and the effect of suppression through Figures 1, 2, and 6.

The paper includes useful empirical analyses, such as loss decomposition showing that forward activation and MLP.ffn2 are most sensitive to quantization, and explores FP6×FP4 precision switching as a promising direction.
Limitations are honestly acknowledged, including the limited compute scale and the lack of hardware speedup evaluation.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is hindered by missing implementation details. No code is released, and Algorithm 2 does not show the actual reset operation—it only states 'return θ' without updating the weights. The outlier channel selection procedure (calibration data, timing, norm computation) is also not fully specified.

The equations for OutControl in Section 5.2 are confusing and appear inconsistent. In the forward equation, both terms use the complement set \bar{A}, and the backward equations for dX do not clearly show how outlier channels are retained in high precision, making the method difficult to reproduce.

The double-block quantization adds a 1×128 outer scale that is not part of the standard NVFP4 format. The paper claims to 'fully leverage hardware support on modern GPUs,' but current NVFP4 hardware does not support two-level scales, and no hardware evaluation is provided. This weakens the efficiency claims and the framing as standard NVFP4.

The experiments are limited to relatively small models (up to 370M parameters) and a single architecture (OLMo-2). Generalization to larger models and other architectures is not demonstrated, although this is acknowledged as a limitation.

The improvements over prior methods, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms. For example, OutControl improves perplexity from 31.49 to 31.28, and some Hadamard ablation differences are small (e.g., 28.47 vs. 28.42).

Some claims are overstated. The assertion of being 'first to analyze and effectively address weight oscillation in low-precision LLM training' overlooks prior oscillation work in QAT and vision transformers, though the LLM pretraining context is new. The '51.3% average reduction' is computed relative to a specific baseline (NVIDIA's recipe adapted to fully FP4) and may not generalize.
The paper does not compare against other recent FP4 training methods (e.g., Wang et al. 2025 [19]) and lacks statistical significance testing for small differences.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: end-to-end 4-bit (NVFP4) fully-quantized pre-training of LLMs, with all three GEMMs (forward, dX, dW) quantized.

The empirical evaluation is broader than typical for this line of work: three model sizes (70M/150M/370M), three token budgets (50B/100B/200B), nine-plus downstream tasks, and several targeted ablations (block size, unbiasedness, Hadamard placement, oscillation methods, outlier selection).

The results are internally consistent and show TetraJet-v2 consistently outperforming Quartet and the NVIDIA NVFP4 recipe across scales on both train/validation perplexity and the downstream average (Tables 1-2).

The oscillation analysis (OsciRisk metric, Figs. 1, 2, 6) is a genuinely useful diagnostic and the paper is plausibly the first to characterize weight oscillation specifically in low-precision LLM pre-training.
The limitations section is honest about the constrained compute budget and the absence of hardware-level speedup measurements, which is the correct treatment of an acknowledged gap.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper itself frames TetraJet-v2 as an extension of TetraJet v1 (switching MXFP4 -> NVFP4 and porting vision-domain ideas to LLMs), and each component is an adaptation of existing work (RHT from [17, 18], oscillation suppression from vision QAT [20, 22, 24], outlier-channel retention from LLM.int8() [27]). The core algorithmic ideas are incremental.

Central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The title/abstract claim 'accurate'/'near-lossless' training with 'minimal impact on task performance,' but a substantial gap to BF16 remains (e.g., 370M validation PPL 25.11 vs 23.70; downstream average 43.60 vs 44.13). This is not lossless, and the framing overstates the result.

Tension with the 'fully 4-bit / fully FP4' framing: OutControl retains ~10% of activation channels in FP8 (or 5% in BF16). This is not a fully-4-bit pipeline, which undermines the stated efficiency motivation and the 'all linear layers in NVFP4' claim.

Downstream gains (Table 2) are within noise: differences between TetraJet-v2-full and NVIDIA/Quartet are well under 1 point on the average, several individual tasks are worse than baselines (e.g., ARC-c 24.75 vs 26.76 for NVIDIA and 28.43 for BF16), and no variance/seed reporting is given to establish significance.

The headline '51.3% gap reduction' is measured relative to the weaker baseline (NVIDIA default) using validation PPL, and the metric is not clearly defined; the absolute gap to BF16 remains large, so the headline figure overstates progress.

No compute-efficiency or throughput evaluation (explicitly admitted), so the primary motivation for 4-bit FQT is unverified; no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the accuracy claims to the algorithm description alone.

Presentation problems: the OutControl forward equation appears garbled (the second term duplicates X_{.,\bar{A}} where it should be the outlier set X_{.,A}), Algorithm 2 omits the actual reset expression, and the definition of the reported gap-reduction metric is left implicit.

Evaluation is confined to a single model family (OLMo-2) and one dataset, and to <=370M parameters; the paper's claims about 'LLM' training are not supported at a scale where 4-bit FQT is actually relevant.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: fully quantized 4-bit pre-training of LLMs using the NVFP4 format, with extensive experiments at three model sizes and three token budgets.
OsciReset is a simple, novel, and empirically effective method for suppressing weight oscillation; Fig. 6 shows oscillation proportion dropping from ~5.6% to ~2.5% after suppression.
OutControl's static outlier channel selection is shown to improve both forward and backward passes (Table 4), and the idea of statically selecting persistent outlier channels is practical.

The ablation studies (Table 3) systematically validate the proposed NVFP4 linear layer design, including the 1x128 outer block, 1x16 weight block, gradient alignment, and the choice to apply RHT only in backward.
The loss decomposition analysis (Tables 5-6) and the FP6×FP4 simulation (Fig. 7) provide useful insights into which quantizers and modules are most sensitive.
The paper includes a limitations section acknowledging compute constraints and lack of hardware speedup evaluation.
weaknesses: The central claim of an 'end-to-end 4-bit FQT method' is not supported: TetraJet-v2-full uses OutControl, which retains selected activation channels in FP8/BF16 and performs high-precision multiplication for dW of those channels (Sec. 5.2). The best results therefore come from a hybrid-precision method, not a fully FP4 one, contradicting the abstract and title. The fully FP4 variant is TetraJet-v2-base, which is less accurate.

No actual speedup or memory-saving measurements are provided, so the efficiency motivation for 4-bit training remains unverified. The authors acknowledge lack of hardware, but this is a major gap for a paper whose primary selling point is computational efficiency.

The experiments are limited to models up to 370M parameters and 200B tokens. While acknowledged, this limits the significance and external validity of the conclusions for multi-billion-parameter LLM pre-training.

There are no error bars or multiple seeds. Many reported improvements are small (e.g., Table 1: 370M validation PPL 25.50 vs 25.11; Table 4: 31.49 vs 31.28), and without variance it is unclear whether they are statistically meaningful.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: NVIDIA's recipe [12] is not fully FP4 (it uses BF16 in some blocks and the final training stage), and Quartet [18] uses MXFP4 rather than NVFP4. Comparing methods at different precision levels and formats weakens the claim of consistent superiority.

The theoretical unbiasedness claim only applies to the base linear layer with stochastic rounding; OsciReset is a heuristic resetting of master weights that can bias optimization, and no convergence guarantee is given for the full method. The statement that the design 'theoretically ensures convergence of SGD' is overstated.

There are presentation and consistency issues: the OutControl forward formula appears to have indexing errors (both terms use the complement set \bar{A}, and the definition of \hat{X} also uses \bar{A}); the oscillation threshold is inconsistent (τ=8 in Appendix A.2 vs OsciRisk>16 in Fig. 6); and key implementation details (e.g., exact timing of outlier channel selection, code release) are missing, hindering reproducibility.
The paper lacks a code release and does not report seeds or variance, making it harder for others to reliably build on the results.

strengths: The paper identifies weight oscillation as a key optimization failure in NVFP4 LLM pre-training and provides empirical evidence (latent weight distributions and trajectories in Fig. 1) showing weights clustering near quantization thresholds.

OsciReset is a simple, low-overhead algorithm that resets oscillating master weights to bin centers; ablations show it outperforms Q-EMA, Freeze, and Dampen and reduces the proportion of oscillating weights (Fig. 7).
OutControl statically selects persistent outlier channels and retains them in FP8, with ablations showing benefits in both forward and backward passes (Table 11).
The paper provides extensive ablations on NVFP4 linear-layer design, including outer-block size, weight group shape, unbiased gradient estimation, and RHT placement (Tables 8, 11, 12).
Efficiency evaluations include CUDA kernel implementations and end-to-end speedups over FP8 on RTX5090 and full Llama2-structured models (1.67x for TetraJet-v2-full).
Limitations and broader impacts are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'fully NVFP4' and 'near-lossless' training is not supported by the best-performing variant: TetraJet-v2-full uses FP8 for 10% of activation channels and high-precision dW for outlier columns, making it a mixed-precision method. The fully 4-bit base still has a substantial gap to BF16 (e.g., 370M validation PPL 25.50 vs 23.70).

Experiments only go up to 370M parameters and 212B tokens. No accuracy results are provided for larger models (1B+), so the claim of accurate NVFP4 training for 'large language models' is not demonstrated at realistic LLM scale.

The NVIDIA baseline is evaluated under a strict fully 4-bit setting that its original recipe was not designed for (it is mixed-precision), which may unfairly disadvantage the baseline and weakens the comparison.

Theoretical claims are overstated: 'unbiased double-block quantization with practically optimal convergence' lacks a convergence proof; the unbiasedness of the gradient estimator relies on independence assumptions that are not fully justified; OsciReset is a heuristic that introduces bias into master weights without convergence analysis.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: the OutControl forward equation has a typo (uses the complement index in both terms instead of the outlier index for the high-precision term); Table 2 is malformed and hard to parse; the code link is missing in the manuscript; no seeds, error bars, or multiple runs are reported.
Hyperparameter sensitivity for OsciReset is only shown at 150M/107B; scalability of the oscillation threshold and suppression start point to larger models and longer training is unknown.
Absolute improvements over prior FP4 methods are modest, and downstream average accuracy still trails BF16 (e.g., 43.60 vs 44.13 at 370M), with several individual tasks underperforming BF16.

strengths: Identifies and empirically characterizes weight oscillation as a distinct optimization failure mode in low-precision LLM pre-training, with concrete trajectory evidence (Fig. 1a/1b) showing latent weights clustering near quantization thresholds as LR decays.

Extensive and well-organized ablations: outer-block size, weight inner-block size (16x16 vs 1x16), unbiasedness/X-alignment/stochastic rounding, and RHT placement (fwd vs dX vs dW) in Tables 8a-c; oscillation-suppression alternatives (Q-EMA, Freeze, Dampen) in Fig. 4; and outlier-selection styles in Table 11.

Runs are non-trivial in token budget (up to 212B tokens on OLMo-2-370M) and include implemented CUDA kernels with measured end-to-end speedups (1.67-1.75x over FP8) and quantified overhead of the finer weight scaling (2.49%, Table 14).

OsciReset is simple, low-overhead (~0.06% training time, ~0.6 bytes/param for the memory-efficient variant), and empirically outperforms prior oscillation methods; the reset-to-bin-center operation leaves the quantized weights unchanged, so it does not immediately degrade the deployed model.
Honest limitations section and reasonable reproducibility artifacts (model hyperparameters in Table 5, technique hyperparameters in Table 6, public code).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to the authors' own prior work: the paper is explicitly a v2 of TetraJet (Chen et al., 2025), and the core recipe is a refinement of NVIDIA's NVFP4 design plus known components (stochastic rounding, block Hadamard/RHT, LLM.int8()-style outlier-channel retention, which is acknowledged). The genuinely new element, OsciReset, is a simple heuristic with no theoretical grounding beyond hand-wavy arguments about 'more chances to be optimized.'

Evaluation scale is small (70M-370M params). The central claim that oscillation is the dominant FP4 failure mode and that the recipe scales is not demonstrated at realistic LLM sizes, and the authors acknowledge this. The 51.3% gap-reduction figure still leaves a substantial residual gap (e.g., 370M: 25.11 vs BF16 23.70).

No error bars or multiple seeds are reported despite small margins (e.g., Table 2 average 43.41 vs 43.60 between base and full, and single-point PPL differences), so several comparisons are not demonstrably above run-to-run noise.

The OutControl forward-pass equation appears erroneous: 'Y = Q_D(X_{:,A-bar}) x Q_D(W^T) + X_{:,A-bar} x Q_D(W^T)' uses the complement set A-bar in both terms; taken literally this would drop the outlier channels entirely. The second term should presumably use X_{:,A}. This is a substantive presentation/derivation error in a central formula.

Notation for the weight group shape is inconsistent across the paper: Sec. 2.3 states Q^(2),Q^(4),Q^(6) use 16x1, Sec. 2.3 point 3 and App. D.1 describe '1x16' vs NVIDIA's '16x16', while Sec. 2.2 introduces a 1x128 outer block. This makes it hard to verify the actual design.

Baseline fairness is questionable. NVIDIA's recipe is evaluated in a non-native fully-FP4 setting that the authors themselves say was designed as mixed-precision, and Wang et al. (2025) is reported at 97.22/82.96 PPL versus ~51/~37 for all other methods (Table 12), which strongly suggests an under-tuned baseline and weakens the comparative claims.

The unbiasedness argument is inherited from TetraJet rather than re-derived; the cross-term behavior of products of independently stochastically-rounded operands (and their scale factors) is not analyzed here, so the 'practically optimal convergence' claim is stronger than the evidence.

Efficiency comparisons are FP4 vs FP8 on consumer RTX5090 hardware; it is unclear how representative this is of data-center NVFP4 block-scaled GEMM throughput, and whether the measured speedup reflects hardware-native FP4 rather than emulation.

strengths: The paper provides a thorough empirical study: it compares against multiple strong recent baselines (Quartet, NVIDIA's NVFP4 recipe, Wang et al., Tseng et al., FourOverSix) under a strict fully-4-bit setting, and backs the design with detailed ablations on block shape, outer-scaling granularity, unbiasedness of gradients, and Hadamard placement (Tables 3, 4, 8, 11-13).

It systematically identifies and targets two distinct, plausibly orthogonal failure modes of low-precision training (weight oscillation and activation outliers), which is a useful framing for the community rather than a single ad-hoc trick.

The methods are well-motivated and mostly principled: the aligned activation in dW, stochastic rounding for unbiased backward estimation, and the dist_Q/dist_M oscillation-risk metric are theoretically grounded and validated empirically (Fig. 4, 7; App. C.3).

Efficiency is demonstrated with real CUDA kernels and end-to-end measurements (Figs. 5, 9; Tables 14-16), showing the finer 1x16 weight scaling adds only ~2.5% overhead and that a 1.67x end-to-end speedup over FP8 is achievable.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: code is released, model/data/technique hyperparameters are listed (App. B), and the full algorithms are given (Algs. 1-4). Limitations regarding model/data scale are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The experimental scale is small (up to 370M parameters, 212B tokens). Claims in the abstract about 'practically optimal convergence in LLM training' and general 'LLM training' are not validated at a scale where the optimization and outlier dynamics could change qualitatively.

Novelty is largely incremental. OsciReset closely resembles prior oscillation handling (Nagel et al. dampening/freezing; Chen et al. Q-EMA/Q-Ramping), OutControl is essentially LLM.int8() static outlier-channel retention extended to training, and the double-block quantizer is a refinement of NVIDIA's NVFP4 scaling recipe with different block sizes.

Some central claims are overstated relative to the evidence, e.g., 'the first effective algorithm to suppress LLMs' weight oscillation bottleneck' and 'practically optimal convergence'; the reported downstream/validation gap to BF16 is still substantial (e.g., 370M val PPL 25.11 vs 23.70).

Internal numerical consistency is imperfect: the abstract's '51.3% gap reduction' does not exactly match the values implied by Table 1 (I compute ~43.6% for 370M and ~51.6% averaged across sizes), and speedup figures vary between 1.67x and 1.75x across sections without a clear reconciliation.

The efficiency evaluation is performed on consumer GPUs (RTX 5090, RTX 6000 Pro) against a TE-FP8 baseline, whereas the practical motivation (FP4 datacenter training on Blackwell) would be more convincingly demonstrated on the hardware where the memory/compute advantage matters most; communication, optimizer, and data-loading overheads are excluded.
